before: its pleasures gone, and alas, only the first echoes still ring! I offer my treasures to an unknown crowd
after: and alas, even the first echo has died away. My song rings out before an unknown crowd
reason: Verklungen explicitly says the echo has faded. The 1808 transcription prints Leid[Lied], indicating song; neither reading says treasures.

before: the clock may stop, its hands may break
after: the clock may stop, its hand may fall
reason: Der Zeiger fallen is a falling hand.

before: I'll wear him down with struggle, with chills, with checks, until, for all his hot and insatiable craving, the dream of a drink will mock his thirsty lips without ever satisfying them. He'll beg for refreshment in vain—had he not already sold himself to the Devil, nothing could save him anyway; he'd still be lost forever.
after: I’ll have him wriggling, freezing, stuck fast. For all his insatiable hunger, food and drink will hover just beyond his greedy lips. He’ll beg in vain for relief. Even if he hadn’t given himself to the Devil, he would still come to ruin.
reason: Speis’ und Trank are both food and drink; zugrunde gehn does not specify eternal damnation.

before: Just follow that old saying, and my cousin the serpent that you were told to crush underfoot: for all your resemblance to God, you'll still end up a sorry specimen!
after: Go on, follow that old saying and my cousin the serpent. One day, being so like God is sure to frighten you!
reason: The devil predicts fear at godlikeness, bange. The crushing underfoot is absent from this speech.

after: [Margaret puts fresh flowers in the pots.]
reason: The German stage direction identifies the person bringing the flowers.

before: as if her feet were fettered and held her back
after: as if she were walking with her feet pressed together
reason: Mit geschlossnen Füßen describes the gait Faust sees. He does not identify fetters.
Rabenstein is the place of execution. The literal raven-stone leaves the setting obscure.

before: I shudder to think of you.
reason: Mir graut’s vor dir is Gretchen’s direct expression of fear toward the man before her.
